nodes.label: Aliasing XOR Mutability
nodes.rationale: Every textbook data structure assumes many mutable pointers into one node graph — precisely what the borrow checker forbids. The five representation strategies are five different answers to how you build a linked structure under this one rule.

nodes.label: Arena + Index Handles
nodes.rationale: An index is not a borrow — that is the whole trick. Arbitrary topology (cycles, back-pointers, cross-links) becomes trivially expressible, plus half the memory (u32 vs 8-byte pointers), contiguity for the prefetcher, Copy handles, and free serialization. The default for this category.

nodes.label: Generational Indices
nodes.rationale: The arena reintroduces use-after-free as a logic bug: a freed-and-reused slot makes an old Handle(7) silently name a different node. {idx, gen} with the generation bumped on reuse converts silent corruption into a visible None at the point of use. 4 extra bytes per handle and slot.

nodes.label: Box Ownership Tree
nodes.rationale: Option<Box<T>> is 8 bytes not 16 thanks to the null-pointer niche, so nullable links cost nothing. The &mut descent compiles because each iteration reassigns the cursor to a borrow derived from the previous one, so only one &mut is ever live.

nodes.label: Recursive Drop Stack Overflow
nodes.rationale: The derived Drop for Box<Node> recurses one frame per link. Measured release, 8 MB main stack: fine at 250,000 nodes, aborts at 300,000 (~30 bytes/frame); a 2 MB spawned thread fails ~4x sooner, so code that survives on main dies in a worker. Fix with an iterative Drop using Option::take(), or an arena where no recursion exists.

nodes.label: Rc<RefCell<T>> Shared Mutable Nodes
nodes.rationale: The closest syntactic analogue to a C pointer, so it is what a C/Java/Python instinct reaches for — and it compiles immediately, which feels like validation. But it converts compile-time errors into runtime BorrowMutError panics, adds refcount traffic, and leaks on cycles without Weak. The borrow checker didn't approve the design; it was turned off.

nodes.label: Slices & Split Borrows
nodes.rationale: Many structures need no nodes at all — heaps, union-find, Fenwick trees, hash tables are arrays with arithmetic. split_at_mut, chunks_mut, and get_disjoint_mut (stable 1.86) prove disjointness statically.

nodes.label: Ord / Hash / Eq Trait Contracts
nodes.source_location: Trait contracts you must not break
nodes.rationale: These are contracts, not just signatures — the compiler checks shape, never semantics. A non-total Ord makes BTreeMap silently lose entries; disagreeing Hash/Eq makes entries unfindable. Floats are the standard trap: partial_cmp().unwrap() panics on NaN, so use f64::total_cmp or ordered-float, and property-test the laws with proptest.

nodes.label: Choose the Hasher by Key Provenance
nodes.rationale: The hasher feels like a global default but is a per-map security/performance trade. Self-generated keys (indices, interned symbols) -> FxHashMap/aHash, measured 4.6-6.0x faster for u32 keys but only 1.2-1.3x for 16-char Strings. Anything attacker-reachable keeps std's RandomState, whose random per-process seed makes precomputed collision attacks impossible.

nodes.label: Miri for Unsafe Structures
nodes.source_location: Raw pointers behind a safe API
nodes.rationale: Not optional for hand-written unsafe data structures: it catches the aliasing mistakes that pass tests, pass code review, and then miscompile under a new optimizer.
